meta.title: Skip the Wrapper
meta.subtitle: Five optimizations measured under fixed semantics. One ships, and it is a packaging change.

abstract: An agent driving a browser through a CLI issues hundreds of sequential commands, so per-call overhead — not per-call work — sets the pace. This study measured five candidate optimizations for one such CLI (Vibium, OSS) across two real journeys under fixed semantics.

Four did not survive. One persistent-process technique lost outright. One was faster only because it stopped checking that elements were actionable — time bought by doing less. One vanished under measurement. The winner turned out not to be an optimization at all but a packaging defect: the command on your PATH is a 41-line Node script that spawns the real binary, so every invocation pays a Node runtime boot first.

introduction.motivation: Agent-driven test automation inverts the usual cost model. A human runs one command and waits; an agent runs a hundred, and the fixed cost of each one dominates. That makes per-invocation overhead a first-class performance property of a CLI — and it is the property nobody profiles, because on a single interactive command it is invisible. The question here is narrow and practical: for one widely used browser-automation CLI, where does the time actually go, and which of the obvious fixes survives contact with a real journey?
introduction.problem: The trap is that almost any change makes a benchmark faster if you let the benchmark change too. Skip an actionability check and clicks get quicker; hold a browser open and startup leaves the total. Neither is a faster tool. So every arm here holds semantics fixed, reports one-time setup apart from the journey, equalises readiness polling, and is compared against a noise floor measured from a control the change cannot have touched. Under those rules, most of the candidates stopped looking like wins.

review.lead: Five techniques, two AUTs, semantics fixed. Absolute milliseconds lead: the same underlying factor measured at two dispatch levels produced ratios differing by 1.85× on identical data, so a ratio without its level is not a result.
review.close: Only T1 is free. It changes nothing about what the tool does — same verbs, same arguments, same actionability-checked click and fill, byte-identical output — because it is not a change to the tool at all. It is a change to how the tool is installed.

experiment.lead: The wrapper is the whole finding. vibium on PATH is not Vibium: it is a Node script that resolves a platform package and execFileSyncs the real native binary. Every vibium <verb> is two process spawns, and the first is a Node runtime boot — paid before any browser work begins.
experiment.measure: On a near-empty command the shim costs ~118ms against ~10ms calling the platform binary directly. The gap is constant whatever the command does, which is what a runtime boot looks like and not what work looks like.
experiment.limit: That per-call figure does not multiply into a journey total. On the flat profile 6 × 106.19ms predicts 637ms against 405ms measured, and the 232ms shortfall is 10.3× the campaign's own 22.6ms single-difference floor. The tax is partly self-refunding: the shim arm arrives at each post-navigate command ~107ms later, and a later-arriving call is a cheaper call.

results.lead: The refund is real, bounded, and its mechanism is only three-quarters of the story.
results.refund_head: The refund shrinks with page weight — but not to zero
results.refund: A falsifier was registered before running: on a page with nothing to hydrate, the refund must vanish. It shrank monotonically with page weight — 82.5ms on a heavy-JS site, 55.2ms on a lighter one, 19.2ms on a bare static page — the mechanism behaving exactly as claimed. But 19.2ms survived, bootstrap CI [+3.3, +22.6], excluding zero. Hydration explains roughly 77% of the effect and is the right account of why it varies; it is not the whole account of why it exists. The prediction failed, and that is the useful part.
results.mapper_head: The residual is Chrome's BiDi mapper, not the page
results.mapper: Chrome's WebDriver BiDi is not implemented in the browser. It is a JavaScript bundle in its own renderer process, a target Chrome names BiDi-CDP Mapper. Probed causally over CDP — which does not queue behind BiDi's own command handling — the mapper's context costs 10.3ms at t=0 and 0.9ms at t=150ms after a navigation, while the page's context, as a control, stays flat. A fixed CPU loop on the page's own clock runs marginally faster right after load, so the page is not computing. The busy thread belongs to the automation layer.
results.patch: The fix is not in the CLI. Resolve bin to the platform binary at install time — hard-link the real binary over the shim in postinstall.js, which is what esbuild already does — and the per-invocation boot disappears. It declines out loud rather than failing: on Windows, under Yarn, or on any link error it prints vibium: keeping the Node shim (<reason>) and leaves a working install alone.
results.patch_verified: 13 runs, 710 reps, 0 mismatches, saving 107.4–111.9ms per call at 40×–60× the measured noise floor. Every sweep was also run in reverse, so a direction effect could not hide in the result.

conclusion.lead: One technique shipped, and the reason it shipped is the transferable part.
conclusion.rule: The cheapest performance win is often not in the code. It is in the packaging.
items: Profile the invocation, not just the operation.
Per-call fixed cost is invisible at n=1 and worth 25–41% of a real journey at n=6–7. Agent workloads live at n=100.
Hold semantics fixed or you are not measuring speed.
The JS-dispatch arm was faster because it stopped checking actionability. Buying time by doing less is not an optimization.
Measure a noise floor from a control the change cannot have touched.
Timing the same arm twice per rep gives what a quiet machine produces when nothing happened — here 2.2ms on the patch sweep and 22.6ms on the campaign. Without it, 108ms is a number, not a result.
~11.6× is a true measurement of a near-empty command and a false claim about real work. The journey figures are 1.33× and 1.69×. A ratio inherits its denominator.
Register the falsifier before you re-run.
The refund mechanism was pushed to a prediction it could fail. It failed, at 19.2ms, and the failure located the residual.
Report the technique that lost, and why.
The persistent-process arm looked obviously right and came in at −740ms. Publishing that is what stops it being retried.
conclusion.close: Filed upstream, at a maintainer's public invitation, as an enhancement in the register the project's own CONTRIBUTING.md asks for — symptom first, patch offered in one line at the end, and an explicit statement of who it does not help: MCP users get no benefit, because that is one long-lived process, and nobody notices 108ms on a single interactive command. It is scripted and agent-driven CLI use where it adds up.

fig1.caption: Journey saving by technique, both profiles, under fixed semantics. Positive is faster. T4 is drawn hollow because its saving is not comparable — it degrades semantics — and T2 is negative on both AUTs.

fig2.caption: The per-call tax by the position of the command in the journey. after_poll is the discriminator: a post-navigate position that pays the full tax, which rules out “post-navigate steps are simply different steps” and leaves the arrival-time refund as the explanation.

diff.file: packages/vibium/postinstall.js — abridged; filed patch at repro:patch/postinstall.diff
lines: +          fs.renameSync(tmp, shim);   // atomic swap, keeps the shim on failure
diff.note: Link then rename, so a failure never leaves a half-written entry point. Every skip path keeps the working shim.

honesty_board.ratio_denominator: ~11.6× is a true measurement of a near-empty command. The journey figures are 1.33× and 1.69×.
honesty_board.retracted_55_180: [RETRACTED] The persistent-process arm previously measured 55–180× on a trivial command; on a real journey it LOSES.
honesty_board.withdrawn_direction_effect: A published ~2.9ms direction effect re-measured at −0.2ms and is withdrawn, in place.
honesty_board.noise_floor_first: The floor is the same arm timed twice per rep — 2.2ms on the patch sweep, 22.6ms on the campaign. The saving is 40×–60× the sweep's.
honesty_board.prediction_before_run: The refund's falsifier was registered first. It fired at 19.2ms, and that located the residual.
